lesson.title: Ablaut Families I: e→i, a→o
lesson.subtitle: geben/gab, sprechen/sprach, fahren/fuhr — the class drills with participles

hook.title: The Family Albums
hook.content: Strong verbs come in families, and the families are recognizable by their melody. Family one: short e in the infinitive becomes a in the past — geben, gab, gegeben. sprechen, sprach, gesprochen. nehmen, nahm, genommen. Family two: long a becomes long u — fahren, fuhr, gefahren. Family three: ä in the du/er present then a in the past, ie in the past of the sleep class — schlafen, schlief, geschlafen. Each family has its English twins standing right beside it: give/gave, speak/spoke, fare/fared, sleep/slept. You are not learning ten verbs. You are learning three melodies that cover them.

footnotes.title: The du/er Vowel Warning
footnotes.content: Some strong verbs change their vowel in the SECOND and THIRD person of the PRESENT too: du gibst, er gibt (from geben); du nimmst, er nimmt (from nehmen). English whispers this once — 'he gives' — German does it visibly. The past-tense melody is unaffected.

pattern.title: Three Melodies, Full Paradigms
pattern.content: Family e→i/a: geben, gibst, gibt, gab, gegeben ↔ give, gave, given. sprechen, sprichst, spricht, sprach, gesprochen ↔ speak, spoke, spoken. nehmen, nimmst, nimmt, nahm, genommen. Family a→u: fahren, fährst, fährt, fuhr, gefahren ↔ fare, fared. The sleep class: schlafen, schläfst, schläft, schlief, geschlafen ↔ sleep, slept. And kommen sits in its own honest corner: kommen, kam, gekommen ↔ come, came, come — the melody you already drilled.
pattern.linguist_note: The du/er present-tense vowel change (gibt, nimmt, fährt, schläft) is i-mutation — the same umlaut that will build plurals and comparatives later. The strong verbs are where it has been hiding all along.

exercises.prompt: Family album one — match the paradigms:
exercises.target_answer: geben / gab / gegeben, sprechen / sprach / gesprochen, nehmen / nahm / genommen, fahren / fuhr / gefahren, fallen / fiel / gefallen, springen / sprang / gesprungen
exercises.meaning: the give, speak, take, fare, fall, and spring melodies
exercises.explanation: e→a in the first family, a→u in the second — the melodies cross the North Sea intact, and fall/spring join the album note for note.

exercises.prompt: 'er _____ ein Bier.' (geben, 3rd person present — mind the vowel!)
exercises.meaning: er gibt ein Bier = he gives a beer
exercises.explanation: geben's du/er present mutates to i: du gibst, er gibt. The past gab is a different note. The melodies keep singing across the album: blasen blies, frieren fror, fliegen flog — the vowel IS the tense.
treten, trat, getreten — tread/trod/trodden, note for note. The e→a melody again.
ge- + the past vowel o + -en: gesprochen — speak/spoke/spoken, note for note.

exercises.target_answer: Er hat mir das Buch gegeben

vocab_hints.note: the receiver takes the dative — mir, the 'give it me' fossil

exercises.explanation: geben, gab, gegeben in a full Perfekt bracket — with the dative mir riding inside: give gave given, to-me.

summary.outcome: Conjugate the e→a and a→u strong families through past and participle.

use_example.german: Er hat mir das Buch gegeben.

summary.takeaway: Three melodies cover a dozen verbs: e→a (geben), a→u (fahren), and the sleep class (schlafen/schlief).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: dachte & the Suppletive Irregulars — think/thought ↔ denken/dachte, where both languages swap in a new past.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Ablaut Families I: e→i, a→o (He gave me the book):
twist.target_answer: Er hat mir das Buch gegeben
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Er hat mir das Buch gegeben" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Ablaut Families I: e→i, a→o without relying on short-term echo.

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

fallen.context_phrase: Das Glas ist vom Tisch gefallen.
fallen.context_translation: The glass fell off the table.
fallen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fallaną; the page lists English fall among the akin forms — a class 7 strong verb on both sides: fell and fiel, fallen and gefallen. [wiktionary]

springen.context_phrase: Das Kind springt über den Bach.
springen.context_translation: The child jumps over the brook.
springen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *springaną (PIE *sprenǵʰ-) — English spring is the documented cognate; strong verb: sprang, gesprungen. [wiktionary]

treten.context_translation: Do not step in the puddle.
treten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *trudaną — English tread is the documented cognate; the same class 5 ablaut: tritt, trat ↔ tread, trod. [wiktionary]

blasen.context_translation: The wind is blowing hard today.
blasen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, a class 7 strong verb (blies, geblasen); the fetched page gives no English cognate, but the standard twin is English blow (blew, blown). [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

frieren.context_translation: Are you cold? I am making tea.
frieren.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *freusaną — the page names English freeze as a cognate; the strong past fror, gefroren mirrors froze, frozen. The German infinitive r spread from the old past forms. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

faust.context_phrase: Er ballt die Hand zur Faust.
faust.context_translation: He clenches his hand into a fist.
faust.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German fūst, from Old High German fūst. English fist is the regular English continuation of this same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

leider.context_phrase: Leider ist das Museum heute geschlossen.
leider.context_translation: Unfortunately the museum is closed today.
leider.etymology_derivation: Originally the comparative of leid (grievous, as in es tut mir leid, I am sorry) — literally more grievously, now simply unfortunately. [wiktionary]

ski.etymology_derivation: A 19th-century borrowing of Norwegian ski, from Old Norse skíð (split stick) - English ski is the same Norwegian loan, and the native German doublet is Scheit (log). [wiktionary][etymonline]

stinken.context_translation: The garbage can stinks in summer.
stinken.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną; the page says compare English stink — the same smell-word with the same ablaut: stink-stank-stunk, stinken-stank-gestunken. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
